title: How a Prince Should Conduct Himself So As to Gain Renown
coreMove: Win esteem through visible enterprises, decisive alignment, and public encouragement while preserving rank.
sourcePressure: The chapter treats renown as something built by great enterprises, striking internal rewards or punishments, open friendship or enmity instead of neutrality, prudent alliances that avoid dependence on stronger victors, support for ability, encouragement of commerce and agriculture, festivals, guild contact, courtesy, liberality, and unchanged majesty of rank.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version becomes personal branding or visibility advice. The writer must show renown as a governing instrument: enterprises occupy rivals, alignment avoids becoming the conqueror's prize, and civic encouragement makes subjects willing to improve without fearing seizure or taxes.

hook: leader announces bold vision at a conference
counterintuition: most people assume neutrality is safe, but actually taking sides wins
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and plan your reputation
pick a side in any conflict

exampleSpecs.domain: a newly crowned inland king opening a long campaign to recover a mountain pass held by raiders
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler whose nobles have been idle enough to plot small innovations against him
exampleSpecs.stakes: the enterprise can found military skill and keep barons occupied, but only if it is more than spectacle
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The king rolls the pass-campaign cord across the noble seating chart and moves every restless baron from court intrigue into named winter supply commands.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A pass-campaign cord lies across a noble seating chart.

exampleSpecs.domain: a harbor duchy choosing whether to stay neutral while two sea powers fight over a strait
exampleSpecs.audience: a duke tempted to avoid present danger by offering neither side arms
exampleSpecs.stakes: the winner will not shelter a doubtful friend, and the loser will not trust a prince who would not court his danger
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The duke folds the neutrality parchment, places his sword token on the weaker ally's strait chart, and writes the reason he prefers shared fortune to being the victor's prize.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A neutrality parchment curls beside a sword token on a strait chart.

exampleSpecs.domain: a city ruler rewarding an unknown bridge mason after a flood repair saves the grain road
exampleSpecs.audience: subjects deciding whether unusual ability is noticed and honored by the prince
exampleSpecs.stakes: public reward for real competence teaches artisans that improving the state brings honor rather than seizure
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince stops the procession at the repaired arch, lifts the mason's measuring chain in public, and grants the workshop tax shield before the guild masters can claim the credit.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A mason's measuring chain hangs from a repaired bridge arch.

exampleSpecs.domain: a grain plain where farmers hesitate to drain new fields because past rulers seized improved land
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince trying to make agriculture grow without lowering his majesty into pleading
exampleSpecs.stakes: fields stay idle if improvement looks like an invitation to confiscation or new taxes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the spring assembly, he nails a no-seizure tablet beside the drainage stakes and then steps back to let the guild wardens record the first claim under his seal.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Drainage stakes stand beside a no-seizure tablet at the edge of a wet field.

exampleSpecs.domain: a border republic deciding whether to ally with a stronger empire against a smaller rival
exampleSpecs.audience: councillors who want the easy alliance but fear becoming subject to the victor
exampleSpecs.stakes: helping a power too strong may destroy the rival and leave the republic at the victor's discretion
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The clerk predicts a clean win, then places the empire's demand seal over the republic's own frontier charter to show what victory may cost.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An empire demand seal rests on the corner of a frontier charter.

exampleSpecs.domain: a canal city holding seasonal boatmen festivals without letting the prince become merely one guild guest among many
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler balancing civic familiarity with unchanged dignity of rank
exampleSpecs.stakes: guilds need visible esteem, but if majesty is abated the festivals stop strengthening rule and start consuming it
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At the boatmen's lantern table, the prince accepts the first cup standing on the dais, then returns the guild ledger with his seal instead of sitting below the wardens.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A boatmen's lantern table glows below a narrow ceremonial dais.

skillTargets: identify visible enterprises that build authority rather than mere spectacle
apply the neutrality versus declared-alignment logic when powerful neighbors fight
analyze alliance choices for lesser-evil risk and dependence on stronger victors
evaluate whether patronage of ability, commerce, festivals, and guild contact preserve rank while encouraging the state

tryThisNowSpec: Choose one public act by a ruler. Classify whether it is a great enterprise, decisive alignment, reward or punishment, economic encouragement, or civic ceremony, then write how it preserves majesty rather than mere popularity.
